records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Budget announcements
VAT and green levies
Some green levies have been taken off household energy bills and moved into general taxation, meaning bill payers may see monthly charges fall.
Which levies are affected?
Net-Zero / Renewable Subsidies: The policy costs and net-zero charges historically loaded directly onto electricity and gas bills—which combined add roughly £180 to an average annual household bill—are being transferred. Five separate green levies on power bills are included in this shifting mechanism. [1]
The Renewables Obligation (RO): This program, the UK’s oldest major green power subsidy, had already seen a 75% reduction on bills under previous emergency measures to move £2 billion to general taxation. The remaining portion is being absorbed by the wider tax pool
As announced in September, the government has cut tax on electricity bills to zero, this VAT cut has been extended until July.
Energy bills
The standing charge on gas bills is being scrapped, the chancellor announced this morning.
About 23 million homes will benefit from removing the levy, which is paid regardless of how much or little gas is actually used.
The Treasury estimates say the removal will lift £45 off an annual bill for 60% of households, as the charge is instead levied on the unit rate.
New energy payment
Twenty million households in council tax bands A to D will get a new £100 energy payment. The Chancellor also urged the Scottish Government to deploy funding to replicate the scheme in Scotland
Heating Oil Market Protections: The UK government introduced stronger regulations for heating oil suppliers, establishing clearer compensation routes, standardized consumer protections, and addressing minimum delivery requirements that previously forced off-grid families to pay large upfront sums

records.bodyText:
Kao Data have launched a ‘Data Centres Explained’ website in partnership with techUK and the Data Centre Alliance. They state they want this site to become a go-to resource for the whole industry — bringing together expertise from across the sector to answer the public’s questions openly and honestly. They are apparently doing this because they believe they need to earn the trust of the public. I took a look at the site and here is my initial assessment - it is a good attempt at corporate greenwashing. Why do I say that? Well for starters look at the picture on the first web page. Apparently this is a data centre; interestingly no megawatt size is provided. This image is totally unrepresentative of the planning applications we are currently dealing with in Scotland for hyperscale data centres which are causing huge community concerns. I would offer this image is a blatant attempt to mislead the public. Next I looked at the FAQ section and clicked on the ones relating to water. This was my response after reading them.
“Unfortunately the answers to FAQ relating to water use will do nothing to allay community concerns. The answers smack of corporate greenwashing. The techUK survey which is often cited by the data centre industry is a flawed survey. It only sampled 12.85% of all data centres within the UK. It is hardly a representative sample of industry practice. It also raises serious questions as to what is the water use of the 87.15% of data centres who did not respond to the survey and why did they not want to respond. The results of this survey cannot and should not be extrapolated to the sector as a whole which is what your answer to the question - Do data centres use a lot of water? - is at risk of doing. A more honest answer would have been - The lack of publicly available data on water use by the data centre industry means it is currently impossible to assess the level of water use at the individual site level or at the industry wide level within the UK.”
I have posted this comment in response to their LinkedIn post where they congratulate themselves for developing this amazing educational resource. I think calling it educational is a long stretch of the imagination. Please feel free to pop along to LinkedIn and offer your feedback because apparently they want to win the trust of the public. From my experience of working in community liaison you do actually need to engage with and listen to communities if you have any hope of building trust.

What the government won't tell you.
#AffordableEnergy #climatechange #Hopetosaveourcountryside #netzero #NationalGrid
BRITAIN’S ELECTRICITY BILLS: THE COSTS THEY DON'T TALK ABOUT
We are constantly told that Britain's high electricity bills are driven by the price of gas. But that is only part of the story.
Behind every electricity bill sits a growing collection of charges, subsidies and payments that most households never see explained.
Look at the figures.
In 2024/25, the Renewables Obligation scheme was valued at £7.7 billion. Transmission charges required another £4.19 billion in revenue, while balancing the electricity system cost approximately £2.7 billion.
Then there are Contracts for Difference, Feed-in Tariffs and Capacity Market payments.
These are different financial measures, and not all are caused by Net Zero. But they are part of the wider cost of Britain's electricity system — and the public deserves to know what they are paying for.
Now look at what is coming.
In 2021/22, Britain's annual transmission revenue requirement was £3.32 billion.
For 2026/27, it is £7.61 billion.
By 2031/32, NESO forecasts £13.80 billion a year.
That is more than four times the 2021/22 figure if the forecast materialises.
And this is before we ask whether the extraordinary reconstruction of Britain's electricity network is delivering value for money.
The National Audit Office has examined a £70 billion transmission investment programme, raising serious concerns about delivery and whether the chosen projects have been demonstrated to offer the best solution.
Ofgem has also rated NESO's evidence of value for money as below expectations.
Meanwhile, across Britain, farmland and countryside are being earmarked for pylons, substations, solar developments and battery installations.
The question is no longer simply how much Net Zero will cost.
The question is whether anyone has properly demonstrated that this enormous programme is the cheapest, most dependable way to meet Britain's actual energy needs.
We should not be spending billions, committing our countryside and passing ever-growing costs to consumers without that evidence being available for public scrutiny.
Our latest investigation looks at NESO's spending, senior remuneration, the grid rebuild and the increasingly urgent question of accountability.
READ THE FULL INVESTIGATION:
https://hopetosaveourcountryside.com/?p=3371
MAKE THEM SHOW THE EVIDENCE.
SIGN THE PETITION TO PROTECT OUR COUNTRYSIDE:
Petition: Suspend Climate Change Act targets & undertake a full national impact assessment
We call on the Government to temporarily suspend the legal duties to meet the UK's statutory carbon budgets and 2050 Net Zero target under the Climate Change Act 2008 until Parliament has considered an independent national assessment of their full costs and impacts.
https://petition.parliament.uk/petitions/780321

It's time to start turning the tide back toward public, municipal, and community ownership of our energy in Scotland.
Whenever we bring this up, people will say things like "energy is a reserved issue."  That's largely true, but here's what they're missing: energy regulation and owning stakes in a wind farm are different! 
ScotGov currently has the power necessary to take public stakes in offshore wind along with supporting more municipal and community energy. So, let's get it done! 
ScotGov has been ambitious in the past with public ownership. We need them to show us that ambition again!

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Herald letters
ROSEBANK is built, crewed and ready to produce. Whilst the public majority is in favour, politicians and activists continue protesting against it, in what feels like a titanic battle over one of the most talked-about UK offshore developments in decades.
International private investors have already spent billions to complete a world-class production facility in over 1,000m of water. With the decision seemingly in the balance, I thought it worth counting what goes down with the ship, should Andy Burnham decide not to start production.
1) Scottish jobs lost: 1,500 to 2,000 (at peak).
2) Lifetime economic contribution to the UK lost: over £25 billion.
3) Global reduction in CO2 emissions, NOX, methane leakage, and microscopic particulate matter: near-zero.
Readers are likely aware that the UK oil and gas industry is in natural decline – most reservoirs are already depleted. It is estimated that 93% of the UK’S total economically viable oil and gas has already been extracted, with North Sea fossil fuel production down by around 74% since the 1999 peak.
Compared to 2026 levels, North Sea production is expected to decline a further 26% by 2030. UK demand will not fall to match, because oil isn’t just what goes in our cars (it’s in our medicines, clothes, toothpaste and, ironically, our solar panels).
Rosebank would meet roughly 8% of the UK’S oil demand.
Where are we, and other users of fossil fuel products, getting the resultant shortfall from? Is it best we further increase our external energy dependency, and ask our friend Vladimir for help?
The UK produces less than 0.8% of the world’s daily oil; 53% comes from the US, Saudi Arabia, China, Russia and Canada combined. In terms of global pollutants, we are not anywhere near the tip of the iceberg. Stopping Rosebank will not change the planet’s course, only the nation’s finances, and for the worse.
The UK energy industry is already taking on water. Unlike James Cameron’s famous film, there is room on the door for both Jack(daw) and Rose(bank). The question is whether the Government will let Rose on. Grant Aitchison,
Aberdeen.
ALEX Orr (Letters, October 27) made some excellent points about energy security. Jackdaw might not help prices but it helps in terms of security. Being selfsufficient in energy is clearly a goal and our wind turbines, solar, hydro obviously help except when nature does not play ball and they cannot be relied on as of themselves.
Sadly, he ignores the safest clean reliable energy of all, nuclear, which of course does not rely on nature. Torness, which has given us 40 years of reliable clean energy, is being allowed to wither on the vine of political dogma.
I wonder if those anti-nuclear politicians will fess up when the wind doesn’t blow and the sun doesn’t shine and the lights go out. I doubt it, because the internet will be down as well.
Ian Mcnair, Cellardyke.

So, the latest report.  Does it live up to the hype which is, and will be, engendered by such statements as:
 "𝐒𝐜𝐨𝐭𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐝’𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐰𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐦𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡, 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝟓𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐣𝐨𝐛𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐥𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 £𝟏𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐮𝐭. 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐨 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞, 𝐢𝐭 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬, 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐲."   ?
That's from Angela Hepworth, the CEO of Scottish Renewables, linking the report's contents to effectively a plea to the Chancellor to put renewables at the heart of today's Budget.
There are caveats given in notes to editors, however.
This is our take on this new report, and it doesn't vary greatly from what we said about the last report.
The headline figures for 2024 are:
• £9 billion direct turnover.
• Approximately 16,800 direct full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs.
• £14.9 billion total economic output, including supply-chain and wage-spending effects.
• £5.1 billion gross value added (GVA).
• An estimated 49,200 FTE jobs supported across the Scottish economy.
However, there are important qualifications.
The 49,200 jobs figure is NOT the number of people directly employed in the renewables industry. It includes 18,275 indirect jobs supported through supply chains and 14,075 induced jobs attributed to wage spending.
The Institute warns that the underlying ONS survey estimates carry considerable uncertainty, particularly for individual technologies. The 2023 and 2024 figures should not be interpreted as a precise measure of year-on-year growth, and results should not be compared directly with previous editions.
There is a further significant limitation. The Institute acknowledges that it currently uses UK industry proportions to allocate Scottish renewable-energy activity across industries, because more recent Scotland-specific data are unavailable. It identifies this as the most significant data limitation in its current approach. The economic model also uses Scottish input-output tables for 2022 and cannot capture structural changes since then.
The reported financial figures are in nominal terms, not adjusted for inflation.
These are estimates of gross economic activity associated with renewable energy. The report does not establish how many jobs are additional to those that would otherwise exist, the net economic benefit to Scotland, or how much of the financial return is retained by Scottish businesses and communities.
This is not a criticism of the Institute for acknowledging the limitations of its research. It has set out those limitations in the report. The question is whether those qualifications receive the same attention when the headline figures are used to support political arguments for accelerating renewable-energy development.
The figures need to be understood in the context of what was measured, how it was estimated, and what remains unknown.
A headline figure is not the whole story; however we can almost guarantee that the industry will try and make it so.

records.bodyText:
SSEN’S FINAL SUBMISSIONS ARE IN — BUT HAVE THEY ANSWERED OUR CONCERNS?
After months of evidence and objections, SSEN’s position remains deeply concerning for everyone living and working along the Tealing–Kintore route.
 LANDSCAPE: Significant visual damage is acknowledged, but the project is still defended on the grounds of national need.
 FARMING: Farmers are expected to adapt machinery and working practices to accommodate the overhead line. But who carries the burden when farming becomes more difficult, costly or dangerous?
 SAFETY: The electrical hazards associated with working beneath overhead lines cannot simply be brushed aside. Farmers and agricultural workers deserve clear, effective protection.
 ENVIRONMENT: Questions remain over landscaping, biodiversity enhancements and when meaningful safeguards will actually be secured.
Our concern is simple: too much of the burden appears to fall on the people and communities affected, while important protections remain contested.
National infrastructure may be necessary, but that does not mean every design should be accepted without proper scrutiny.
Our farms matter. Our landscapes matter. Our communities matter.
The Reporters must weigh the claimed national benefits against the real consequences for rural Scotland.
 OUR RURAL COMMUNITIES DESERVE FAR BETTER.
Please share this post. The voices of our rural communities must continue to be heard.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Scotsman letters
The Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh says that she is “minded” to refuse Rosebank Oil Field, although she has agreed to the operation at the Jackdaw Gas Field, she is “less keen on the larger oil field”.
We can only wonder why. Drilling for our own oil gives us greater security of supply and helps our balance of payments with foreign producers.
Also, it does not increase the greenhouse effect. We still need oil for the gearboxes of the wind farms, for plastics and fertiliser manufacture all of which are vital for our modern life, and we will have to import oil from a foreign country.
No other country in the world would countenance this decision, as they all place their economy before any thoughts of the green lobby.
That is a win, win situation and hopefully the Government will reflect on this before making a final decision.
James Macintyre Linlithgow, West Lothian 
There has been much rejoicing, correctly, at the decision to grant approval for the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. For decades, the whole of the United Kingdom has benefited from this essential industry, employees, families, businesses large and small.
The recent procrastination by both Scottish and UK governments over supporting North Sea oil and gas has had a hugely detrimental effect on Aberdeen and the North East and is reducing the economic benefit to the country.
The blinkered attitude of green zealots who believe oil and gas production can be switched off with an immediate benefit from renewables is laughable.
Globally, oil will be required for decades and North Sea production can assist the big picture. Yes it may go to Rotterdam or wherever to be processed but the refined product comes back for our considerable benefit.
A decision on the essential Rosebank field is due soon. That one person, an energy secretary, has the sole decision-making power on approval of this vital field is a scandal.
One person who has no real experience or involvement in the business determining the financial futures of families affected, of small businesses in the supply-chain is not acceptable and must be reviewed.
Our prime minister must take responsibility of this and grant approval of Rosebank for the benefit of the whole country.
Douglas Cowe Newmachar, Aberdeenshire

The European Commission has given the Go Decision for EURO-TIDES, clearing the landmark project to move into construction.
The tidal energy array project, being led by Orbital Marine Power, developer and operator of the world’s most powerful tidal turbine, will be deployed at the European Marine Energy Centre (EMEC) Fall of Warness tidal energy site in Orkney Isles.
The go decision marks a major milestone for the European Commission Horizon Europe funded project, first announced in October 2023. Having successfully passed a formal review of its engineering, permits and financing, EURO-TIDES has now been approved to move into construction, with Orbital targeting deployment in 2028, subject to completion of its current 
investment round.
The array will be made up of four turbines – three of Orbital’s next-generation O2-X turbines and one O2 – built and connected to operate as a single coordinated tidal energy farm. It will be the first time Orbital turbines have been deployed and operated together as a connected array, representing an important milestone in the company’s journey towards commercial scale tidal energy deployment.
Once operational, the array is expected to generate enough clean, predictable power for around 9,200 homes, with each O2-X capable of supplying approximately 2,400 homes. Together, the array will generate enough electricity to power the equivalent of around 85% of households in Orkney.
The European Commission has identified the transition from individual tidal turbines to connected, multi-turbine arrays as one of the defining milestones in the commercial development of the sector. EURO-TIDES will help prove that multiple turbines can be built, connected and operated together reliably and at scale. By demonstrating the next stage of industrial deployment, the project is expected to strengthen confidence across investors, insurers, policymakers and the wider supply chain, helping accelerate tidal energy’s route to commercial maturity.
This achievement shows how European public investment is turning innovation into industrial reality. Tidal energy is ready to contribute to the objectives of the European Green Deal and Europe’s climate neutrality ambitions by delivering predictable, home-grown renewable power that strengthens energy security and complements wind and solar.
The next challenge is clear, turning successful flagship projects like EURO-TIDES into a pipeline of commercial deployments across Europe. With the right market framework and continued policy support, Europe can remain the global leader in tidal energy, delivering economic growth, industrial leadership and clean, secure energy for Europeans.
EURO-TIDES is being delivered in partnership with CWD (Center for Wind Power Drives, RWTH Aachen), EMEC, Énergie de la Lune, ENGIE Laborelec, MaraSoft, Ocean Energy Europe, the University of Edinburgh, and Orbital Marine Power.
The project aims to demonstrate the reliable deployment and operation of connected tidal turbine arrays at commercial scale, helping reduce the cost of tidal energy, strengthen manufacturing capability and supply chains, build confidence among investors and insurers, and support a future European pipeline of more than 2 GW of tidal energy projects.
The European Marine Energy Centre operates the Fall of Warness grid connected tidal test site off the west coast of the island of Eday in the Orkney Island. Located in a narrow channel between the Westray Firth and the Stronsay Firth.
The site features strong marine currents
reaching up to 4 metres per second (about 8 knots) during spring tides.
￼Test berths range from 12 M to 50 M deep across an area of approximately 2 to 9 square kilometres. The site offers eight grid-connected test berths, each linked by an 11 kV subsea cable to an onshore substation at Caldale on Eday.
The location is managed by EMEC with a Crown Estate Scotland lease running through 2040.The site has hosted multiple full-scale marine energy prototypes, including OpenHydro's early design and Orbital Marine Power's O2 tidal turbine.
The O2 turbine was constructed in Dundee, by Texo Group. The hull was produced by Grey Fabrication in Cupar, and the four composite blades were manufactured by A C Marine & Composites (ACMC) in Gosport.The entire structure was then protected from the elements out at sea by BROL-Coat Ltd. They gritblasted everything before applying over 4000 litres of paint, ultimately adding an extra 4t in weight.— at Eday Island.

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
WINTER ELECTRICITY SECURITY - ARE WE BEING GIVEN THE FULL PICTURE?
We're still working through evidence concerning the operation and security of Britain's electricity system, and this latest article by Kathryn Porter raises further questions.
NESO says Britain should have sufficient electricity supplies this winter, with a reassuring margin of spare capacity.
But Kathryn questions how robust that assessment really is.
In simple terms:
Wind power: NESO has changed the way it calculates how much reliable capacity wind can provide, producing a more favourable headline figure.
Electricity imports: The assessment assumes that Britain can draw on electricity from other countries when needed, even though those countries may also be short of power.
Getting electricity to consumers: The calculations do not account for regional grid constraints that can prevent available electricity from reaching where it is needed.
The combined risks: Low wind, reduced imports and unexpected power station outages could occur together, rather than separately.
Kathryn's illustrative calculations suggest that, under a more cautious set of assumptions, NESO's published 5.9 GW spare capacity margin could fall to around 0.5 GW  -  before allowing for grid constraints.
That is not a prediction of an impending shortage. It is a warning about how much the reassuring headline figure depends on the assumptions behind it.
There are wider questions here about how electricity security is assessed, how uncertainties are communicated, and whether the risks are being given sufficient attention.
More to follow on the subject.

records.bodyText:
Inch Cape Offshore Wind Farm will generate enough green electricity to power the equivalent of more half the homes in Scotland and at 1100 MW will be Scotland’s largest offshore wind farms.
Located 15 Km from the Angus coast, the project is on a site covering 150 square kilometres and will feature 72 wind turbines and a single offshore substation. The power it generates will be transported via two 85 kilometre export cables to a new substation being built on the brownfield site of the former coal-fired Cockenzie Power Station on the East Lothian coast. From here it will connect to the national transmission network at an existing grid substation.
Inch Cape was first considered in 2008 after the site was secured in The Crown Estate’s third leasing round auction. Since that time, the wind farm ownership has changed along with its design, which has evolved to take advantage of new technologies and innovations as the offshore wind industry has developed.
Since its original consent was received in 2014, these changes included an updated wind farm design which reduced the number of turbines to 72, and an increase in generation capacity enabling adoption of the latest technology within existing consent requirements. The project will use 15MW Vestas turbines, sitting on a mix of jacket and monopile turbines which will be some of the deepest ever installed. At the heart of the wind farm will be a Siemens Energy Offshore Transmission Module on a 68m deep jacket foundation, fabricated at Smulders’ yard in Wallsend.
The project reached financial close in January 2025 and is now in its offshore construction phase, with marshalling ports in Leith and Dundee and construction being operated out of Montrose. It is due to be completed in 2027.
Inch Cape is owned by Inch Cape Offshore Limited (ICOL) – an equal joint venture between ESB and Red Rock Renewables.
January 2026 Inch Cape’s first batch of 15 transition pieces has arrived at the Port of Leith in Edinburgh in readiness for installation offshore later this year.
Each transition piece is around 28 metres tall, roughly the height of an eight-storey building, has an outer diameter of 8.3 meters, and weighs approximately 600 tonnes.
Inch Cape will have a total of 54 transition pieces, each individually designed and engineered by renewables engineering consultancy SLPE specifically for its corresponding monopile foundation.
The transition pieces will provide a stable interface between the project’s XXL monopile foundations, which will be piled into the seabed, and the wind turbine towers placed on top. Each transition piece will be secured to a monopile with a bolted connection and then grouted. The wind turbine tower will then be installed and bolted on top.
The transition pieces feature a boat landing system, access ladder and external work platform enabling Inch Cape’s technicians and engineers to enter the wind turbine tower for maintenance activity during the operational phase of the project. 
Internally, the transition pieces have four platforms at different levels. At their base is an air-tight platform, next a cable hang-off platform which supports the inter-array cables, then an entrance platform with elevator access to the wind turbine and nacelle unit. Finally there is a bolting platform for the construction crew to access and safely work from as they bolt the transition piece and turbine tower interface flanges.
The transition pieces are painted an industry-standard bright-yellow to ensure visibility at sea and comprise sacrificial anodes for cathodic protection, to prevent steel corrosion in the harsh marine conditions.
The first batch of CWHI-fabricated transition pieces were transported by COSCO heavy-lift vessel Hua Sheng Long and arrived at the Port of Leith. They will be installed by marine contractor Seaway7 using the vessel Alfa Lift .
The transition pieces are clearly visible at the Port of Leith awaiting delivery to the Windfarm site, a few photos taken today.
The onshore substation for the project is located on the old Cockenzie Power Station.— at Port of Leith.
